analysis.trend_summary: The Eswatini dataset is dominated by macroeconomic indicators (55 data points) with almost no conflict/unrest, humanitarian, or investment data (only 2 investment records, no ACLED-type events, no OSINT signals). What is visible shows a small, low-inflation economy with moderate and improving GDP growth (3.6% in 2025, projected 4.0% in 2026 per IMF), rising but still moderate public debt (44.9% of GDP in 2025 to 50.0% projected 2026, IMF), and persistently very high unemployment (34.6% in 2024, 34.2% in 2025, World Bank). Investment activity on record is limited to two greenfield private infrastructure projects — a $115M solar plant (2021) and a $17.2M telecom project (1998) — both financed by "Private sector" per World Bank PPI. The complete absence of conflict, protest, or humanitarian event records means no security or political-stability pattern can be derived from this dataset; this is a data-coverage gap, not evidence of stability.
analysis.security_analysis: No security or conflict events are present in the supplied data (zero entries in the conflict/unrest feed). This precludes any assessment of a security risk driver from this dataset; the absence of recorded events should be read as a data gap rather than confirmation of a benign security environment.
analysis.political_stability_analysis: The data contains no protest, civil unrest, or political-violence-targeting-civilians events for Eswatini in this window, and no humanitarian/OSINT signals were returned. As with security, this reflects an absence of coverage in the supplied feeds rather than a substantiated finding of political stability; no trend can be characterized from this dataset.
analysis.economic_analysis: IMF figures show real GDP growth accelerating from 3.6% (2025) to a projected 4.0% (2026), alongside low and stable inflation (3.1% in 2025, 3.5% projected 2026). The current account balance is projected to remain in modest deficit (-0.6% of GDP in 2025, -1.8% in 2026 per IMF), a reversal from the 1.6% surplus recorded by the World Bank for 2024. General government gross debt is on an upward trajectory, rising from 44.9% of GDP (2025) to a projected 50.0% (2026, IMF), while World Bank data shows total external debt stock at $1.24B (2024). Unemployment remains structurally very high and essentially flat, at 34.6% (2024) and 34.2% (2025, World Bank), indicating growth is not translating into labor-market absorption.
analysis.investment_analysis: Recorded investment activity is sparse, limited to two World Bank PPI Database greenfield projects: a $115.0M solar electricity plant (Frazium) marked active as of 2021, and a $17.2M ICT/telecom project (MTN Swaziland) dating to 1998 and also listed active. Both are attributed to "Private sector" financiers with no bilateral or multilateral development-finance institution (e.g., DFC, AfDB, World Bank IBRD/IDA lending) appearing in the activity log. FDI net inflows were recorded at 1.6% of GDP in 2024 (World Bank), consistent with a modest but non-zero level of foreign private investment, though the dataset does not show recent (post-2021) project-level investment activity.
key_relationships: - The only identified active investment actor is "Private sector (World Bank PPI Database)," linked to 2 projects spanning 1998 (MTN Swaziland telecom, $17.2M) and 2021 (Frazium solar plant, $115.0M).
- IMF macro series (BCA_NGDPD, GGXWDG_NGDP, PCPIPCH, NGDP_RPCH) show a consistent multi-year projection set for 2025-2026, indicating growth (3.6%→4.0%) alongside rising debt (44.9%→50.0% of GDP).
- World Bank labor and FDI indicators (SL.UEM.TOTL.ZS, BX.KLT.DINV.WD.GD.ZS) for 2024-2025 show high unemployment (~34%) persisting despite positive FDI inflows (1.6% of GDP, 2024).
risk_flags: - Government gross debt projected to rise sharply from 44.9% (2025) to 50.0% of GDP (2026, IMF), a notable one-year increase warranting monitoring.
- Current account balance swings from a 1.6% of GDP surplus (World Bank, 2024) to projected deficits of -0.6% (2025) and -1.8% (2026, IMF), suggesting a deteriorating external balance trend.
- Structurally high unemployment (~34%, World Bank 2024-2025) persists despite reported GDP growth, indicating limited labor-market responsiveness to growth.
- No security, political-stability, or humanitarian data are present in this dataset, meaning conflict and unrest risk cannot be evaluated and should not be assumed absent.
analysis.data_caveats: This dataset contains zero conflict/unrest, humanitarian, or OSINT events for Eswatini, so no security or political-stability conclusions can be drawn — this is a coverage gap, not a finding of stability. Investment data is limited to only two projects (1998 and 2021), with no entries for the past several years, so current investment/development-finance activity cannot be characterized with confidence. Economic indicators for 2026 are IMF projections rather than realized outcomes and should be treated as forecasts.
